auditor_value: In the train frame, along the incline (down-slope) m(g sin30° + a) = 10 N, normal to it mg cos30° = 8.66 N ⇒ tanφ = 2/√3 ⇒ φ ≈ 49.1° from the normal to the ceiling; T = √175 = 5√7 ≈ 13.2 N

findings.note: The printed expression mg sin30°·(1/2) equals mg/4 = 2.5 N, not √3mg/4 = 4.33 N. The horizontal component of the pseudo force m(g/2) directed down a 30° incline is (mg/2) cos30° = √3mg/4. The number carried forward is right but the written equation is false; a student who copies and evaluates it gets Fx = mg/4 and T = √26·mg/4 ≈ 12.7 N.

findings.quote: Adding only gravity and the pseudo force's along-incline component without resolving into ground-frame horizontal and vertical parts gives the wrong tension.
findings.note: The pseudo force lies entirely along the incline, and resolving gravity and the pseudo force along and normal to the incline (no ground-frame resolution at all) gives T = m√((g sin30° + a)² + (g cos30°)²) = 5√7 N and the angle 49.1° directly. The entry condemns a correct alternative method and names no wrong number.
findings.fix: Adding the magnitudes of gravity and the pseudo force as scalars, T = mg + ma = 15 N, instead of adding them as vectors (they are 60° apart), which gives T = 5√7 ≈ 13.2 N.

notes: Independent solve in incline axes agrees with the solution's final answer (49.1°, 5√7 N). The ground-frame route is valid; the angle bookkeeping (19.1° backward from vertical + 30° forward tilt of the ceiling normal) is correct. common_mistakes[1] (30° − 19.1° = 10.9°) computes as stated.
